shipped.title_o: The dynamic interplay between goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning: A computational modeling approach.
shipped.authors_o: Lin; FitzGibbon; Theobald; Breitwieser; Brod; Murayama; Sakaki
shipped.outcome_quote: Robustness: Methodologically, we show that the WAIC criterion used in the original study exhibits poordiagnostic reliability and is theoretically biased for autoregressive panel models. We implementexact leave-future-out cross-validation as an unbiased alternative, under which the original modelselection conclusions are no longer supported.

blind_target.authors: Lin, W. M., FitzGibbon, L., Theobald, M., Breitwieser, J., Brod, G., Murayama, K., & Sakaki, M.
blind_target.title: The dynamic interplay between goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning: A computational modeling approach.
blind_target.evidence_quote: We reanalyzed the publicly available Study 1 data from Lin et al. (2026).
blind_target.outcome_computational_quote: Our Stan implementation differed only in computational details, most notably the use of a non-centered parameterization to improve sampling efficiency; the underlying mathematical model is equivalent, and the recovered parameter estimates closely reproduced the original results.
blind_target.outcome_robustness_quote: We reanalyze the Study 1 data by introducing a log(trial) learning curve into the best-fitting model. The negative emotion-to-performance effect is no longer credible in this extended model; instead, a strong practice effect emerges.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Equivalent original models recover the original estimates; adding a practice curve removes the credible negative emotion effect, and time-respecting validation challenges original model selection.

shipped.title_o: Re‐Assessing Elite‐Public Gaps in Political Behavior
shipped.outcome_quote: Computational: The study was already successfully reproduced by Institute for Replication collaborators. || Robustness: Overall, we conclude that Kertzer's Claim 1 survives an evaluation of whether each study should be included and survives the pooling of similar treatments.

blind_target.title: Re-Assessing Elite-Public Gaps in Political Behavior.
blind_target.evidence_quote: For our robustness replication of Claim 1, we evaluated the decision to include studies and study treatments in the meta-analysis given the criteria Kertzer lays out and whether the results are robust to other reasonable decisions about inclusion.
blind_target.outcome_computational_quote: To answer this question, we replicate Kertzer’s (2022) Figure 1 in our Figure 1(a). Each estimate shows the absolute value of the difference between the mass and the elite Average Treatment Effects (ATEs) with 95 percent confidence intervals.
blind_target.outcome_robustness_quote: Only a small number of the these 162 treatments significantly affected masses (N=28) or elites (N=30). This low rate suggests the possibility that almost all of these experiments failed to successfully manipulate either masses or elites. If so, we may not be able to conclude that masses and elites respond similarly to experiments with confidence until political scientists produce more experiments with actual treatment effects or with successful manipulation checks in cases of null effects. More studies with successful manipulations are necessary to get a better answer.
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Their own Figure 1(a) reproduces the original estimated differences and Figure 2 original-results counts match 39/162 and 19/162. This is independent of the note that I4R collaborators had previously reproduced the study. Inclusion and pooling checks preserve Claim 1, but conditioning on successful manipulations substantially increases elite-public differences and materially qualifies the central inference, as emphasized in the conclusion. The conceptual check of Claim 2 supports the original, but uses the control samples already present in the original meta-analysis; no fresh data collection is reported.
